I’m happy to report that Invisible Thread — a new musical that opened Wednesday night at Second Stage (which is near, but not on, Broadway) and marks her latest transfer — is a high-energy, visually arresting, well-intentioned bust.

The latest of them, Invisible Thread, isn't the most successful; in fact, it has some pretty big issues that cry out to be addressed. But it dares to take on a difficult, complex subject, and it has an enormous heart -- qualities that money can't buy.
Invisible Thread has several moments of emotional uplift, and is likely to send at least a portion of the audience enthused out into the night.
Still, despite its virtues, the musical is a bit too much of a slender “Thread” to deserve such a first-class treatment.

This is a genuinely appealing show even if the storytelling is a little muddled.
Earnest and energetic, tuneful and often joyful, Invisible Thread also tries, like its protagonists, to make a difference.
Yet I can’t shake the feeling that this really is more of a project than a show.
The musical doesn’t dig very deep, but it’s food – comfort food to be sure – for thought.
INVISIBLE THREAD is nothing if not energetic, colorful, and spirited while also finding room to be poignant and uplifting.

cn.t: This earnest, autobiographical musical about an American actor volunteering in Uganda draws praise for its sincerity and energy, though critics are divided on its execution—some find it affecting and joyful, others deem it lightweight and self-focused.
